s: is_a state of happiness [attained through gain] Heaven is represented by gain in the merchants' parable and is associated with increasing one's capital through eminent virtues.

teaches death with one's will [as the better kind of death] The Law of Compassion teaches the better kind of death. A wise man who chooses it becomes calm through patience and keeps an undisturbed mind at death.

is_a ascetic The False Ascetic is concerned with those who acknowledge bondage and liberation in words but do not abstain from sins or act according to their beliefs. Such people seek comfort in mighty words and mistakenly believe themselves wise while sinking through their sins.
Truth is knowledge of reality; ignorance brings pain, while seeking and embracing it makes one wise and bends zeal.

affects all men ignorant of Truth [throughout endless Samsâra] All men who are ignorant of the Truth are subject to pain. People suffer for their own deeds, and those attached to their bodies, colours, and forms will reap pains.

leads_to birth [through its ways] A wise man considers the ways that lead to bondage and birth. Recognising the truth about bondage and liberation, he should choose what is beyond and above this world.

is_feared the two sons of Bhrigu [along with old age and death] Birth is regarded as part of the precarious and transitory condition of human life. Fear of birth, together with old age and death, motivates the characters to abandon worldly life.
Sixth Lecture urges kindness to all creatures: recognizing their self-love, cease depriving, endangering, and combating them.
An alms-bowl holds food an ascetic eats to preserve life, while the ascetic wanders without desires and keeps no store, even grease.

Sin causes descent through endless Samsâra and arises from injury to living beings through ignorant ritual practice. Abstaining from it is necessary for liberation, while fools persist in it. Hatred and lust ensnare sinners, but Harikêsa avoids sin through guarded thought, speech, and body and rejects violent ritual acts.
Death, awaited by an ascetic after recognising Karman’s cause, harasses mankind and compels immediate adoption of the Law.
Arhat Gñâtriputra, venerable native of Vaisâlî, speaks Sixth Lecture teachings and possesses the highest knowledge and faith.
is_a lecture The Seventh Lecture teaches through parables that human life is precious capital and that conduct determines whether one reaches heaven, hell, or another state.

l: Parable of the Ram, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: is_a parable The Parable of the Ram compares an animal raised for a guest and then killed with an ignorant great sinner who lives for pleasures but gains life in hell.
A ram, an animal, is raised, fed rice and gram, and fattened for a guest, then killed and eaten when the guest arrives.
causes_death_of ram [by arriving after the ram has been fattened] The guest is the person for whose arrival the ram is raised and prepared. Its arrival causes the ram to be killed and eaten.

An ignorant great sinner commits many harmful acts: killing, lying, robbery, theft, deception for plunder, pursuit of women and pleasures, drinking liquor, and eating meat. Through sinful conduct he longs for and ultimately attains hell. At death, burdened by Karman and grieving, he unwillingly goes to the world of the Asuras, a dark place, or is born in hell.
is_represented_by heaven [in the merchants’ parable] Gain represents heaven in the parable of the three merchants.
Loss of capital results from losing human life through sin, leading to birth in hell or as a brute animal.

is_forfeited_by ignorant great sinner [through slavery to lusts] Divine life and its pleasures surpass human pleasures a thousand times and more. Losing divine life, as well as human life, leaves a person in states of misery.

are_surpassed_by divine pleasures [by a thousand times and more] Human pleasures are limited and brief compared with divine pleasures. They are compared to a drop of water at the top of a blade of Kusa-grass when set against the ocean.
Three merchants set out with capital: one gains, one merely returns it, and one loses it; their journey explains the Law through human life, heaven, and loss.

The soul’s benefit and eternal welfare matter most: a person avoids hatred and lust, while a monk protects the soul through meditation, discipline, restraint, and freedom from attachment; souls sullied by many sins hardly attain Bôdhi.
teaches Law of ascetics [with pure knowledge] Kapila of pure knowledge taught this Law. Those who follow it will be saved and gain both worlds.

saves those who follow it [and gains both worlds for them] The Law of ascetics teaches that killing of living beings should not be permitted and that a monk should practice careful conduct. Kapila taught this Law, and those who follow it will be saved and gain both worlds.

are_like beasts [when ignorant of the prohibition of killing living beings] Some who call themselves Sramanas are like ignorant beasts because they do not know the prohibition of killing living beings. Those stupid sinners go to hell through their superstitious beliefs.
cross Samsâra [as merchants cross the sea] Pious ascetics (sâdhu) can get over the impassable Samsâra as merchants cross the sea.

increase_with means [the more one gets, the more one wants] Desires increase with a person's means, and greater possessions produce greater wants. Even when two mâshas would supply a need, a person would scarcely think ten millions sufficient.

King Nami, a Kshattriya ruler of Videha and royal Seer, remembers his former birth, becomes enlightened as a Svayamsambuddha, and ends delusion. After placing his son on the throne, he retires from the world, relinquishing Mithila, his army, seraglio, retinue, wealth, and pleasures. Directed by Sakra to humble himself, he rejects arguments for royal power, punishment, conquest, and sacrifice, teaching self-control, patience, austerity, and self-conquest before taking Sramanahood.

Sakra, king of the gods, comes to King Nami disguised as a Brâhmana and questions Mithilâ’s uproar. He urges Nami toward royal and worldly duties, then reveals himself, recognizes Nami as blemishless, praises and reveres him, and flies away; he also directs Dasârnabhadra to renounce the world.
Mithilâ, a town and country containing the sacred tree Manôrama, erupts in uproar during Nami’s retirement; amid fire, Nami compares the noise to storm-shaken birds and claims nothing of his burns.
Blessed by pure birth and knowledge, the Brâhmanas tend sacrificial fire, mock and expel Harikêsa, then seek forgiveness, feed him, and ask proper sacrifice.
Pravragyâ is King Nami’s excellent retirement stage, whose occurrence causes uproar in Mithilâ.

follows King Nami [after he enjoyed pleasures] Nami becomes enlightened after enjoying excellent pleasures with the beautiful ladies of his seraglio. He gives up those pleasures and becomes a Svayamsambuddha in the true Law.

l: Nami's retirement from the world, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: involves lonely place [as a place of resort] Nami retires from the world after placing his son on the throne and giving up Mithilâ, his army, seraglio, and retinue. He resorts to a lonely place and takes upon him Sramanahood.

l: The Leaf of the Tree, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: The Leaf of the Tree is the subject of the comparison with a fallow leaf that falls when its days are gone. It illustrates the brevity and ending of human life.

Gautama enters the houseless state, is urged to be careful, wipe off sins, abandon attachments, and follow the right path. Having crossed the great ocean, he hears the Buddha’s well-delivered sermon, cuts off love and hatred, and reaches perfection.

The soul may inhabit earth, water, fire, wind, vegetable, and various sense-organ bodies for periods ranging from seven or eight births to endless time, and may remain a whole life as a god or denizen of hell. Through carelessness and good and bad Karman, it is driven through Samsâra. It has no corporeal form, cannot be apprehended by the senses, and is therefore eternal. Bad qualities cause its fetter and worldly existence, though one teaching says it is produced in the body.
The houseless state is Gautama’s condition after leaving wife and wealth, with a warning not to return to vomit.
The great path is the path from which the thorns have been cleared. Gautama is told to walk in the right path and not take an uneven road.

l: the world of perfection, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: The world of perfection is a place of safety and perfect happiness, reached through perfected saints’ religious practices; Kitra attains its highest place after highest self-control and indifference to pleasure.

l: the road of peace, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: The road of peace is what the enlightened and liberated monk should preach to all. It is associated with control and liberation.
The text says that there is now no Gina, but there is a highly esteemed guide to show the way. It also refers to the Buddha as the source of a well-delivered sermon.

l: the Buddha's well-delivered sermon, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: is_adorned_by illustrations The Buddha's well-delivered sermon is adorned by illustrations. Having heard it, Gautama cut off love and hatred and reached perfection.

Perfection is taught by Ginas and reached through compassion, Sânti, or renunciation, self-restraint, austerities, and freedom from defilement and Karman; Gautama reaches it after cutting off love and hatred, attaining safety and perfect happiness.
is_highest highest truth The seeker after the highest truth is instructed to study the sacred lore in order to cause himself and others to attain perfection.

Harikêsa-Bala, born in a family of Svapâkas, becomes a chaste, self-controlled monk and sage. He practices mendicancy, penance, Samitis, and Guptis, owns no property, and receives food after a month’s fast. At a Brahmanical sacrifice he is mocked and beaten while begging, yet remains without hatred, accepts apology and food, and teaches true sacrifice and purity.

is_a sacrifice [tended by Brahmanas] Harikêsa approached the enclosure of a Brahmanical sacrifice while begging. Its priests claimed that the food was prepared exclusively for themselves and used the occasion to reject and assault him.

l: Yaksha of the Tinduka-tree, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: Yaksha lives in the Tinduka-tree, compassionately becomes invisible to defend Harikêsa-Bala, then Yakshas assist him and repel young attackers.
Bhadrâ, king Kausalika’s daughter and the Purôhita’s wife, protects Harikêsa-Bala by stopping angry young men, warning against harming the ascetic, and leading Brahmanas to appease him.
is_parent_of Bhadrâ [father] King Kausalika had given his daughter Bhadrâ to Harikêsa, but Harikêsa would not accept her.

assault Harikêsa-Bala [with sticks, canes, and whips] At the teachers’ command, many young men beat Harikêsa with sticks, canes, and whips. Yakshas and Asuras then drove them off and caused them to suffer, after which they bowed and sought protection.

has_value no value [compared with penance] The Brahmanas rely on pure birth and knowledge to claim superiority, but Harikêsa teaches that angry, violent, lying, thieving, property-owning people are bad fields regardless of their status. The gods proclaim that birth is of no value compared with penance, citing Harikêsa, the son of a Svapâka.

is_produced_by benevolence [as the return for gifts] Harikêsa compares the recipient of a gift to a field that may return merit, as farmers sow corn hoping for a return. He teaches that the saints, who call at both high and lowly houses, are blessed fields.

Celibacy is a holy bathing-place, clear for the soul, where Harikêsa becomes pure and removes hatred or impurity. It is realised through ten conditions that protect against sensuality and doubts about chastity.

l: injury to living beings, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: is_a sinful_action [when inflicted on living beings of the six orders] Harikêsa teaches that the proper sacrifice involves doing no injury to living beings of the six orders. He says that using Kusa-grass, sacrificial poles, straw, and wood, together with ritual actions, injures living beings.

are self-control [together with right exertion and tranquillity] Harikêsa teaches that self-control, right exertion, and tranquillity are the oblations praised by the sages. He calls abandoning the body in purity and without attachment the great victory and best of offerings.
Bathing is praised as true purification in the Law through celibacy, cleansing the soul and removing hatred or impurity beyond water washing.

Sambhûta, once a Kândâla contemptuously treated in Hastinâpura, resolves to become a universal monarch. Born later as Brahmadatta in Kâmpilya, he reunites with Kitra, receives wealth, yet as king pursues sinful sensual thoughts and ultimately sinks into hell.

Kitra, born to a merchant family in Purimatâla, enters the order after hearing the Law, becomes a monk indifferent to sensual pleasures, advises Brahmadatta to abandon them, practices excellent conduct, penance, and highest self-control, and reaches perfection.

Brahmadatta, born of Kulanî in Kâmpilya, is the powerful king of the Pañkâlas with five beautiful palaces. Though knowing the Law, he rejects Kitra’s counsel and clings to sensual pleasures, ending in the deepest hell.

is_where the sinful resolution [is taken by Sambhûta] Hastinâpura was where Sambhûta, in a former birth, saw the powerful king Sanatkumâra and formed his sinful resolution out of desire for sensual pleasures.
Kâmpilya is a town where Brahmadatta is born, Sambhûta and Kitra reunite to recount actions’ rewards, and Sañgaya rules and hunts in Kêsara-park, meeting an ascetic.
has_king Brahmadatta [a powerful and prosperous king] The Pañkâlas were ruled by Brahmadatta, who was called their king and was urged to abandon transitory pleasures.

is a hard thing [for those attached to sensual pleasures] Renunciation is presented as difficult for those attached to sensual pleasures. Kitra urges Brahmadatta to choose it for the sake of the highest good.
is_entered_by Kitra [after hearing the Law] The order is the path Kitra entered after hearing the Law and the path he urges Brahmadatta to enter for the highest good.

is_to_become a universal monarch [in some later birth] The sinful resolution was formed by Sambhûta in Hastinâpura from desire for sensual pleasures and was to become a universal monarch in a later birth.

is_a town [ancient, wealthy, famous, and beautiful like heaven] Ishukâra is an ancient, wealthy, and famous town described as beautiful like heaven. Several beings born there remember former merit, abandon worldly pleasures, and take refuge in the path of the Ginas.
King Ishukâra abandons kingdom and pleasures after Kamalâvatî teaches the Law, enters monastic life with her, and reaches perfection.

is_wife_of king Ishukâra Kamalâvatî is the wife of King Ishukâra. She rejects the world and its pleasures, urges the king to abandon his kingdom and property, and becomes a nun before reaching perfection.
Bhrigu, a Brahmanical Purôhita married to Yasâ and father of two sons, becomes a mendicant after his sons become monks and eventually reaches perfection.

l: the two sons of Bhrigu, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: Bhrigu’s two dear bachelor sons remember former austerities, reject worldly and Vedic pursuits, become virtuous Sramanas seeking liberation, and attain perfection with their parents and a royal couple.
Domestic life, a householder’s impermanent existence, is rejected by Bhrigu and his sons, who abandon family, property, pleasures, and duties for liberation.

is_caused_by the fetter of the soul Worldly existence is caused by the soul's fetter and is continued by attachment to pleasures. The characters seek to end it through renunciation and correct understanding.
The world, consumed by love and hatred, is unstable and dangerous; attached beings miss this, while its perils lead characters to withdraw.

l: the end of misery, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: The end of misery is attained by those overcoming doubts, realising Bhâvanâs, and practising the Law; the king, queen, Bhrigu’s family reach it after enlightenment or entering the order.

Nirgrantha is a monk defined by disciplined renunciation. He adopts the Law to live with fellow-monks, abandons former friends, desires, love, delusion, house, and ties, and wanders as an unknown beggar. Upright, righteous, sinless, versed in sacred lore, and devoted to protecting his soul, he controls thoughts, words, acts, and senses; keeps vows; practises austerities and self-discipline; meditates on the soul; endures heat, cold, and lowly lodging; and expects neither hospitality nor praise. He avoids sins, harm, worldly arts, divination, medical treatment, gain from householders, and praise of social groups or artists. Content with little food and even unappealing fare, he is not angry when offerings are withheld. The account then gives specific safeguards for solitary chastity and freedom from sensual attachment: he avoids unsuitable resting places, women, cattle, and eunuchs; does not converse, sit, observe, listen to, or recall pleasures connected with women; and rejects rich food, excess, ornaments, and pleasant sense objects. These precautions preserve chastity, rules, health, and faith.
is_a lecture The Sixteenth Lecture presents ten conditions for the realisation of celibacy and verses explaining the same discipline. It concludes by affirming the Law proclaimed by the Ginas.
Venerable teachers declare ten conditions for realizing celibacy, whose understanding helps monks advance in self-discipline, Samvara, contemplation, and guarded conduct.
Pleasant things include sensory enjoyments, food, ornaments, conversation, company, and women's charms; they are hard to abandon and likened to Tâlaputa poison for seekers of the true Self.
is_a lecture The Seventeenth Lecture teaches about The Bad Sramana. It distinguishes the conduct of a bad monk from that of one who avoids sins and is pious among his brethren.

is_a Sramana [bad] The Bad Sramana sleeps, eats, and drinks as much as he likes, neglects learning and discipline, disrespects his preceptor and teachers, harms living beings, and acts carelessly. He may be deceitful, talkative, arrogant, greedy, quarrelsome, improperly fed, attached to householders, or devoted to heretical teachers and fortune-telling. He is despised in this world like poison and is nobody in this world and in that beyond.
A Nirgrantha enters an order, learns Law, receives discipline, and attains difficult Bôdhi, but may afterward live as he likes and become a bad Sramana.

Sramana is a religious figure whose bad form is defined by comfort-seeking, neglect of learning and discipline, disrespect for preceptor and teachers, and lack of self-control. He harms living beings, seeds, and sprouts; uses furnishings carelessly; moves hastily; inspects inattentively; quarrels and perverts truth. He neglects austerities, eats improperly, leaves his preceptor for heretics, changes school, and lives by fortune-telling. Yet when pious among his brethren, he avoids these sins, is welcomed like nectar in this world, and conquers both this world and the next.

The bad monk is a Sramana who appears to be a monk but fails to protect himself from sins like heretics. Lowest among worthy brethren, he is despised like poison and has no status in this world or beyond.

Sañgaya, a Gôtama, is king of Kâmpilya with numerous troops and war-chariots. After descending from Brahmalôka and having been a god in Mahâprâna heaven, he hunts in Kêsara-park, kills a deer seeking refuge, learns the Law from Gardabhâli, renounces power, becomes a monk, and knows soul and life hereafter.
A venerable houseless ascetic studies sacred texts, meditates on the Law, practices self-control, and teaches a king after a deer’s killing about transience, cruelty, Karman, and penance.
Gardabhâli, a venerable monk and Sañgaya’s teacher, knew sacred lore and good conduct; Sañgaya adopted the Ginas’ faith before him.

is_abandoned_by Sañgaya [upon adopting the faith of the Ginas] Kingly power is portrayed as transient and ultimately something that must be abandoned. Sañgaya and many other kings gave it up and entered the ascetic order.
An ocean- or earth-girt kingdom, Bharatavarsha is abandoned by rulers who renounce worldly life.

The king is warned that wives, children, friends, and relations will not follow him in death, while others may enjoy the riches and wives he leaves behind. A king should therefore practise penance, abandon cruelty, and renounce worldly power.

l: royal renunciation and entry into the ascetic order, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: Royal renunciation places a son on the throne, abandons royal power and pleasures, and enters ascetic order, undertaken by Maghavan, Udâyana, Sañgaya, and other kings.

These records summarize the later lectures of the Uttarâdhyayana, a religious teaching centered on renunciation, self-control, destruction of Karman, and liberation from Samsâra. It begins with exemplary lives: Balasrî renounces kingship, Samudrapâla becomes a monk after witnessing punishment, Arishtanêmi abandons marriage after seeing animals destined for slaughter, and Râgîmatî and Rathanêmi return to the Law through austerity. King Srênika is converted by a saint’s teaching, while Kêsi and Gautama reconcile the laws of Pârsva and Vardhamâna, with Kêsi accepting the five vows. Gayaghôsha rejects ritual status as the measure of true Brâhmanahood and leads Vigayaghôsha into monastic discipline. The lectures then prescribe monastic practice: Samitis, Guptis, correct daily conduct, care for living beings, confession, meditation, alms-seeking, austerities, and obedience to the Guru. Garga’s comparison of bad bullocks and bad pupils warns against laziness and disobedience. Doctrinal sections define the path as right faith, knowledge, conduct, and austerity; explain righteous exertion, penance, causes of bondage, the chain of delusion, and the eight kinds of Karman. They also describe the six Lêsyâs, whose bad forms lead to misery and whose good forms arise from discipline and lead to happier states. The conclusion describes the houseless monk’s renunciation of possessions and sensuality, divides the world into living and nonliving things, classifies beings from perfected souls to immovable and movable creatures, and presents perfected souls as dwelling at the top of the world. Across the whole work, disciplined renunciation and knowledge culminate in release, beatitude, and freedom from transmigration.

Balasrî, also called Mrigâputra, is a crown-prince living in Nandana. After recalling a former birth and understanding vows and suffering, he rejects pleasures, renounces property, enters the Sramana order, practises austerities, and reaches perfection.

Sramana is an ascetic, saint, and houseless monk defined by restraint, concentration, penance, self-control, virtue, and freedom from property and egoism. After giving up household life and taking Pravragyâ, he observes the five great vows and five Samitis, is protected by the three Guptis, and renounces attachments, wealth, possessions, desire, love, greed, and worldly success or failure. He protects living beings, prevents and destroys bad Karman through discipline and austerities, while recognizing that misery and happiness arise through his own self. His path requires constant exertion concerning vows, senses, conduct, duties, living beings, faults, scriptures, and other prescribed points. He seeks righteousness through study, pondering the Sûtras, serving teachers, choosing wise company, eating permitted food in proper measure, and living alone in suitable, pure, quiet places. He restrains his senses and tongue, avoids pleasures, women, trade, construction, cooking, fire, possessions, praise, and comforts; instead he lives on carefully begged alms and meditates only on true things. He bears calamities well, remains detached from pleasant and unpleasant things, and maintains chastity. At death he rejects food and drink, leaves the human body, and is liberated from misery. Through sustained austerity and freedom from Âsravas, he obtains absolute knowledge, eternal beatitude, release from Samsâra, and Nirvâna.

The Sramana order demands difficult vows: impartiality, non-injury, truthfulness, non-stealing, chastity, non-possession, fasting, and endurance. It confers Sramana status through equanimity. Mrigâputra enters with parental permission; Gayaghôsha urges Vigayaghôsha to renounce attachments and enter.

The five great vows are strict, demanding duties for ordained monks, observed by Mrigâputra after entering the order. They require lifelong nonviolence, truthfulness, non-taking, chastity, and non-possession: not killing, lying, stealing, being unchaste, or holding property. Carelessness prevents complete release from fetters and failure in life’s battle.
The five Samitis are disciplines of walking, speech, begging, handling necessary articles, and disposing bodily waste; broadly, they include the three Guptis.
Guptis are three disciplines of mind, speech, and body, preserving chastity by preventing harmful desires, thoughts, speech, and actions.

The Law is a dharma practiced to avoid future suffering, become free from Karman, and reach Nirvâna. Its highest form is that of Kâsyapa, or Rishabha, and it requires self-control, penance, right conduct, faith, knowledge, meditation, equanimity, chastity, non-violence, truthfulness, non-possession, and freedom from attachment. It is a car that may yoke bad pupils, yet it inspires liberation, turns the soul from worldly pleasures toward houseless life, and through study and sincere practice destroys ignorance and Karman. It is loved and meditated upon with the Lêsyâs, Samitis, and Guptis.

Samsâra is a beginningless, endless, fourfold realm of worldly existence, portrayed as a large and dreadful ocean, a mine of dangers, and a wilderness of old age and death. It contains living beings who have not reached perfection and is marked by repeated births, deaths, misery, dangers, and a long succession of pains. Attachment to pleasure keeps beings wandering within it. Those who long for liberation fear it, while indifference to sensory objects can leave one unaffected by its pains. Souls cross Samsâra through liberation, correct behaviour, religious exercise, beneficial modes of life, abandoning worldly undertakings, destroying Karman, and following the road to perfection. Perfected souls have crossed its boundary and are free from transmigration.

Karman is a powerful, eightfold cause of bondage, suffering, worldly existence, birth and death. It binds souls to transmigration and is connected with merit and demerit: it may be meritorious or sinful, while bad Karman arises from love, hatred, delusion, and sinful, uncontrolled, or worldly activity. Originating in delusion, it also produces love and hatred, six Lêsyâs, and the conditions by which the soul is affected by sins. Acquired across millions of births, its eight kinds keep the soul turning in the Circle of Births, with their subdivisions, atoms, places, durations, and development explained. Yet its influx through bad channels can be prevented, and it can be destroyed by observance of the Law, self-purification, conduct, control, study, austerities, renunciation, concentration, pure meditation, self-control, and penance. With no bad influx and through dispassion, the soul annihilates Karman and becomes exempt from transmigration.

Nirvâna is the great happiness and final deliverance toward which the Law leads: freedom from pain, perfection, and an eternal safe, happy, quiet place free from old age, death, disease, and sorrow. It is difficult to approach, but great sages and self-subduing ascetics reach it through simplicity, right knowledge, faith, conduct, austerities, ending activity, and destroying Karman. Those who attain it end transmigration, the stream of existence, misery, and all sorrow.
A place of retribution for sinful monks and forbidden-alms takers, hell inflicts extreme heat, cold, and brutal punishments, suffering far worse than the human world.
Former birth as a Sramana is recalled upon seeing one, prompting rejection of pleasures and pursuit of renunciation.
Mrigâputra renounces power, possessions, family, and property with parental permission, enters the Sramana order, observes great vows, and lives without attachment or egoism.
Mrigâputra, famous through austerities, purifies himself by religious practice and severe fasting, then reaches perfection, liberation, and Nirvâna.
A wild animal lives and roams alone in forests, finding food and drink in woods and lakes while healthy; when sick, no one cures or feeds it, exemplifying an independent monk’s life.

A pleasant painted house, secured by doors and adorned with white ceiling-cloth, garlands, and frankincense, increases desire and passion; its construction kills living beings, so a monk should neither build it nor cause it to be built.
The body is an impermanent, impure, transitory vessel of suffering that must be left behind; it is also a boat crossing the Circle of Births, reaching the opposite shore only if it does not leak.

Pleasures are portrayed as beautiful or pleasant in appearance but painful in effect: like poisonous Kimpâka fruit and glue. Attachment to them causes passions, misery, soiling, and wandering in Samsâra. Mrigâputra gives them up after reflecting on continuous suffering; Râgîmatî rejects Rathanêmi’s urging to enjoy them. The enlightened turn away, and one seeking liberation avoids fixing thoughts on pleasant sensory objects or turning the mind toward unpleasant ones.

Misery is an affliction of mankind, characterizing Samsâra through birth, old age, disease, and death, especially hell. It arises from birth and death, attachment, aversion, desire, and sensory pleasures. It ceases with ignorance and delusion; dispassion, the Law, and the road of the wise lead to freedom and liberation.

l: the flood of old age and death, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: Old age and death endanger the world, consume it, and carry away living beings. Making Samsâra a wilderness of danger, their flood drives Mrigâputra toward renunciation and the Law, portrayed as an unflooded island, refuge, and shelter.

is_given_to Balasrî [to enter the order] Mrigâputra's parents warn him that Sramana duties are extremely difficult, but ultimately grant permission for him to enter the order. After making them repeat their permission, he gives up his property and goes forth.

Tapas are austerities practised by monks after being decided upon, particularly when avoiding neglect of self-control. They are twofold, external and internal, and each kind is sixfold. They matter because, together with control, they bring purity, destroy Karman, and are one of four causes of final deliverance. Monks consider their austerities after night duties, undertake them, and praise perfected saints. The records illustrate severe penance through Mrigâputra’s vows, meditation, purification, and monthly fast, and through Garga’s departure from laziness to lead a virtuous wandering life.

Mrigâputra gives up his fields, house, gold, power, wealth, servants, family claims, and all other property. He renounces possessions permanently, as a snake casts off its slough. A monk should have no property and should be indifferent to dirt and gold. He should not desire gold or silver or engage in buying and selling.

l: The Great Duty of the Nirgranthas, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: is_a sermon [great and extensive] The Great Duty of the Nirgranthas is preached by the saint as a sermon on protection, self-control, observance of vows, and liberation. It teaches that those who possess virtuous conduct and destroy their Karman will reach the permanent place.

The Nirgranthas follow doctrines centered on great vows, penance, self-control, and correct behavior; careless or sensual followers fail, while strict practice frees them from sinful influences and crosses Samsâra.

King Srênika, ruler of Magadha with wealth, horses, elephants, subjects, power and command, encounters a saint. He first offers worldly protection and pleasures, then hears the teaching, understands being without protection, seeks forgiveness, and becomes a staunch believer in the Law with his household.

is_a town [among towns what Indra is among the gods] Kausâmbî is the town where the saint's wealthy father lived. During his childhood there, the saint suffered a severe eye-disease, burning fever, and intense bodily pains.

The Ginas are teachers with the highest road, abandoned by self-willed sinners pursuing pleasure. Possessing the best knowledge, they teach final deliverance, six kinds of substances, nine truths, and the Law of monks. They prescribe precepts and exertion in righteousness; following and adoring the twenty-four Ginas purifies faith. They also describe Îshatprâgbhâra as an open umbrella.

The Circle of Births is an endless cycle of repeated pain, like an ocean, in which the soul turns round and round while bound by Karman. A saint seeks escape by becoming a houseless monk and ceasing action. Through thorough, pious practice of the creed of the Ginas, people become pure and free from passions; the omniscient Gina and great sages bring the cycle to an end.

is self-protection [attained through becoming a calm, restrained, houseless monk] Protection is explained as something not supplied by wealth, rulers, physicians, parents, siblings, or spouses. A person becomes the protector of himself and others through his own conduct, while his own Self is the doer and undoer of misery and happiness.

l: the Law of the Nirgranthas, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: The Law of the Nirgranthas is harmed by sensuality and neglect, but properly followed it destroys Karman and leads to the greatest permanent place.
A severe illness beginning in childhood brought eye-disease, burning fever, and dreadful pains; physicians, family, and wife could not relieve it, but sleep made the pains vanish.
The saint’s ordination begins the morning after his pains vanish: he leaves his relations, becomes a calm, restrained houseless monk, and becomes protector of himself and all living beings.

is_a lecture The Twenty-First Lecture tells the story of Samudrapâla, his renunciation of household life, and his practice of the Law of monks. It teaches how restraint, endurance, and detachment lead beyond worldly existence.

Samudrapâla, a Srâvaka’s son, grew up comfortably in Kampâ, married Rûpinî, and learned seventy-two arts. Seeing a condemned man led him to houselessness; he practised monkhood, endured calamities, annihilated Karman, and attained Nirvâna.
is_a town Kampâ was the town where Pâlita lived and where Samudrapâla was raised.
Pâlita is a merchant and Srâvaka, Mahâvîra’s disciple, who travels by boat to Pihunda for business, marries a merchant’s daughter, and heads toward Kampâ.
Mahâvîra, a noble venerable Ascetic of the Kasyapa Gôtra and a disciple’s teacher, delivered The Exertion in Righteousness.
Law of monks, taught by Ginas, requires five great vows and teaches compassion, restraint, endurance, detachment, and sensory control.

Monks are houseless, well-disciplined practitioners whose creed centers on compassion, forbearance, chastity, abstaining from sin, and control of their senses. They walk carefully, speak blamelessly and concisely, avoid faults in begging, and inspect and handle their outfit, almsbowl, mouth-cloth, broom, and cloth with care. They practise Samitis, Guptis, tenfold correct behaviour, study, meditation, confession, Kâyôtsarga, and prescribed duties through day and night. They endure pleasant and unpleasant conditions, praise and blame, dangers, and bodily and mental difficulties without fear or improper replies. Having abandoned household life, property, egoism, passions, attachments, and Âsravas, they follow discipline, the Law, renunciation, control, and austerities. Through conduct and discipline they destroy Karman, obtain perfection, attain final liberation, and reach eternal beatitude.
Calamities are dangerous, dreadful, and difficult to bear, caused by gods, men, or animals; a steadfast monk endures them fearlessly like an elephant in battle.

is_an ocean-like Flood Worldly existence is described as an ocean-like Flood to which beings are exposed, along with distress, delusion, fear, and attachment. Samudrapâla crossed it after freeing himself from fetters and annihilating his Karman.

Rathanêmi, a monk, prince, and Samudravigaya's son, is disturbed after seeing Râgîmatî and asks her to be his lover; rebuked, he returns to the Law, practises self-control and asceticism, annihilates Karman, becomes Kêvalin, and reaches highest perfection.
Vasudêva, powerful king of Sauryapura and husband of Rôhinî and Dêvakî, fathers Râma and Kêsava, blesses Arishtanêmi, and urges Râgîmatî toward Samsâra's crossing.
asks_in_marriage Râgîmatî [for Arishtanêmi] Kêsava asks for Râgîmatî in marriage for Arishtanêmi. He travels with the wedding procession and returns to Dvârakâ after Arishtanêmi renounces.
Samudravigaya is Sauryapura’s powerful king, husband of Sivâ, and father of Arishtanêmi and Rathanêmi.

Arishtanêmi, Gautama’s black-skinned, powerful son of Samudravigaya and Sivâ, is a saviour and lord of ascetics, honoured by Dasârhas and linked to Vrishnis. En route to marry Râgîmatî, he sees animals for slaughter, renounces, becomes a Kêvalin, and reaches highest perfection.

Râgîmatî, a virtuous, learned king’s daughter and intended bride of Arishtanêmi, renounces after his ordination, leads others into the order, defends her vows against Rathanêmi, undertakes severe austerities, annihilates Karman, becomes a Kêvalin, and reaches highest perfection.
Gods are living beings with five senses, divided into Bhaumêyikas, Vyantaras, Gyôtishkas, and Vaimânikas, with subdivisions and lifespans described.
Animals are movable organic beings, classified by senses, kinds, habitats, durations, bodily continuance, and confinement for slaughter and consumption.
is_city_of Dasârhas Arishtanêmi leaves Dvârakâ on an excellent palankin and ascends mount Raivataka. After honouring him, Râma, Kêsava, the Dasârhas, and many people return to Dvârakâ.
Raivataka is the mountain Arishtanêmi ascends after leaving Dvârakâ. His renunciation takes place in a park there, and Râgîmatî later travels toward the mountain.

l: marriage of Arishtanêmi and Râgîmatî, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: Arishtanêmi and Râgîmatî’s planned marriage ends when Arishtanêmi renounces after seeing animals kept for slaughter.
Arishtanêmi renounces after learning animals are kept for his wedding food, leaves Dvârakâ, ascends Raivataka, plucks his hair, and enters the order.

is_chosen_by Râgîmatî [after Arishtanêmi's ordination] Râgîmatî renounces after hearing that Arishtanêmi has become ordained. She cuts off her hair, enters the order, and induces many relations and servants to enter it as well.

leads_to highest perfection [after severe austerities] Rathanêmi and Râgîmatî practise true Sramanahood and severe austerities throughout life. Their practice leads them to become Kêvalins and to reach the highest perfection.
Highest perfection is reached as Rathanêmi, Râgîmatî, Gayaghôsha, and Vigayaghôsha become Kêvalins and annihilate Karman through self-control and penance.
Pârsva is a thoroughly enlightened, omniscient Gina, Arhat, and prophet of the Law, whose teaching recognises four vows and permits under and upper garments.

Kêsi is a young Sramana and famous disciple of Pârsva, accomplished in sciences, right conduct, and Sruta and Avadhi knowledge. Residing in Tinduka park, he arrives at Srâvastî, questions Gautama about two Laws, resolves his doubts, and sincerely adopts the five vows.
Vardhamâna, a venerable Gina and Prophet of the Law, is world-known; through Gautama, his Law mandates five vows and monastic nudity.

Gautama is Vardhamâna’s famous, enlightened disciple, complete in sciences, right conduct, and knowledge of the twelve Aṅgas. Residing in Kôshthaka park, he conquers foes, fetters, and love of existence through discipline. He arrives at Srâvastî and answers Kêsi’s questions about two Laws and overcoming spiritual dangers.
Srâvastî is a town reached by Kêsi and Gautama during their wandering; its district contains Tinduka and Kôshthaka parks.
The Tinduka park in the district of Srâvastî is where Kêsi takes up residence. Gautama later goes there with his pupils to meet Kêsi, and Kêsi adopts the Law of the five vows there.

l: the Law of Pârsva, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: recognises the four vows [but four vows] The Law of Pârsva recognises four vows and allows an under and upper garment. Gautama explains that its difference from the Law of Vardhamâna arose because the capacities of beings differed across the ages.

l: the Law of Vardhamâna, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: enjoins the five vows [five vows] The Law of Vardhamâna enjoins five vows and forbids clothes for a monk. Kêsi adopts this Law after Gautama resolves his doubts.
pursue the same end [as the five vows] The four vows are recognised by the Law taught by Pârsva. They are presented as pursuing the same end as the five vows.
pursue the same end [as the four vows] The five vows are enjoined by the Law taught by Vardhamâna. Kêsi sincerely adopts this Law after the meeting with Gautama.

The Tîrthakaras use superior knowledge to establish what carries out the Law, introduce outward marks for religious recognition, and teach knowledge, faith, and right conduct lead to final liberation.

l: the disciples of Kêsi and Gautama, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: Disciples control themselves, practise austerities and virtues, then question right Law, conduct and doctrines, prompting Kêsi and Gautama’s meeting.

l: clothing rules for monks, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: The clothing rules contrast Pârsva’s permitted under and upper garments with Vardhamâna’s prohibition; Gautama says outward marks aid religious life and recognition but do not cause final liberation.

l: knowledge, faith, and right conduct, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: are_causes_of final liberation [true causes] Knowledge, faith, and right conduct are taught to be the true causes of final liberation, rather than outward marks.

The Self is the one invincible foe, though Gautama says he has vanquished it with the four cardinal passions and five senses. It advances through desire for the Law, right faith, discipline, knowledge, conduct, concentration, control, austerities, repentance, confession, devotion to the Guru, and freedom from greed and passion. It purifies faith through adoration of the twenty-four Ginas, destroys and cuts off Karman, and gains absolute knowledge and faith. After pure meditation and destroying remaining Karman, it obtains perfection, enlightenment, deliverance, unchecked happiness, and final beatitude. Renouncing its bodies, it reaches the highest region, develops into its natural form, and ends all misery.
are four [anger, pride, deceit, and greed] The cardinal passions are anger, pride, deceit, and greed. Together with the Self, they form five foes that Gautama says he has vanquished.

The five senses are foes whose desired objects cause passions and pain. Unrestricted eating strengthens their fire, while dispassion avoids harm; Gautama says he regularly vanquished them with the Self and cardinal passions.
The ten foes are the Self, four cardinal passions, and five senses; Gautama says vanquishing one and then five vanquishes all ten.

include love, hatred, &c. [heavy fetters] Fetters bind living beings. Gautama says that he has cut off and destroyed all fetters by the right means and is therefore set free; love, hatred, and attachment are described as fetters.

is a dreadful plant [brings forth dreadful fruit] Love of existence is the dreadful plant that grows in the innermost heart and brings forth dreadful fruit. Gautama says he has torn it out completely with its roots and therefore lives pleasantly.

l: the fire of the passions, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: is the passions [burns embodied beings] The fire of the passions burns embodied beings. Gautama says it is extinguished by knowledge, a virtuous life, and penances, which he compares to water.

l: knowledge, virtuous life, and penances, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: are water [extinguishes the fire of the passions] Knowledge, a virtuous life, and penances are the water that extinguishes the fire of the passions. Gautama says that sprinkled with the drops of knowledge, the fire does not burn him.

The mind is an unruly, dreadful, bad horse, governed by Gautama through the Law and knowledge. Attached to pleasures, it is attacked by love and hatred; recognizing desire’s vanity brings indifference. Living simply and subduing senses protects it from Love, while purity makes it proficient in meditation and concentration.

is_taught_by Ginas [most excellent path] The right path is the path taught by the Ginas and is described as the most excellent path. Gautama knows both the right and wrong paths and therefore does not go astray.

l: the Law as refuge, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: is the island [firm ground and most excellent shelter] The Law is the island and firm ground that provides refuge and excellent shelter from the flood of old age and death.
Life is the sailor crossing the ocean of the Circle of Births, present in perfected souls and discussed through beings’ and bodies’ durations.

has_ended the Circle of Births [brings light into the whole world of living beings] The omniscient Gina is compared to the spotless sun that illuminates the whole world of living beings. He has put an end to the Circle of Births and brings light to the world.

l: the meeting of Kêsi and Gautama, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: In Tinduka park at Srâvastî, Gautama resolves Kêsi’s doubts about two Laws and practice; Kêsi adopts five vows, elevating knowledge and virtuous conduct.
is_a lecture The Twenty-Fourth Lecture concerns the Samitis and Guptis and explains their place in the creed.
The creed has eight articles, consisting of five Samitis and three Guptis. The eight Samitis are said to comprehend the whole creed taught by the Ginas and set forth in the twelve Aṅgas.

is_a Samiti [going by paths trodden by men, beasts, carts, &c., and looking carefully so as not to occasion the death of any living creature] The îryâ-samiti requires going by paths trodden by men, beasts, and carts while looking carefully to avoid causing the death of any living creature.

is_a Samiti [gentle, salutary, sweet, righteous speech] The bhâshâ-samiti requires gentle, salutary, sweet, and righteous speech. A well-disciplined monk should use blameless and concise speech at the proper time.
is_a Samiti [receiving alms while avoiding forty-two faults] The êshanâ-samiti governs receiving alms in a manner that avoids the forty-two faults that are laid down.

is_a Samiti [receiving and keeping necessary religious articles after careful examination] The âdâna-samiti governs receiving and keeping things necessary for religious exercises after carefully examining them.

is_a Samiti [performing the operations of nature in an unfrequented place] The ukkâra-samiti governs performing the operations of nature in an unfrequented place. The place should meet various conditions that support self-control and avoid harm to living beings.

Mano-gupti is Gupti that restrains the mind from sensual wandering through contemplation, study, and similar activities, while preventing sinful, harmful desires and thoughts that bring misfortune, misery, or destruction to living beings.
vâg-gupti is Gupti that prevents sinful speech, beginning with silence and similar practices and extending to speech expressing harmful desires or acts causing misery or destruction to living beings.
A Gupti that fixes the body in an immovable posture, as in Kâyôtsarga, preventing bodily actions from expressing harmful desires or causing misery or destruction to living beings.

Walking is a disciplined monk’s practice, pure in cause, time, road, and effort: grounded in knowledge, faith, and right conduct; done by day; avoiding bad ways and sense objects; and maintained through attentive focus on each step, body, and path.

has_objects food, articles of use, and lodging [three kinds of objects] Begging requires avoiding faults in the search for, receiving, and use of food, articles of use, and lodging. A zealous monk should avoid faults caused by the giver or receiver, faults inherent in receiving, and four faults in using the articles received.
A monk practice performed day and night despite pain, followed by reflection on transgressions and confession concerning knowledge, faith, and conduct.
A monk who lives on alms should beg rather than buy. Living on alms is described as benefitting, and the monk should collect alms in small parts while avoiding faults.
Religious exercise uses five Samitis to practice religious life and Guptis to prevent sin; a sage mastering them crosses Samsâra, compared to traveling in a car, beyond the Circle of Births.

Gayaghôsha, a famous Brâhmana and houseless monk, practices the yamas, subdues his senses, and wanders. In Benares he fasts, calmly endures refusal of alms, teaches true sacrifice, Brâhmanahood, and liberation, and urges Vigayaghôsha to enter the order. Through self-control and penance, he annihilates Karman and reaches highest perfection.

Vigayaghôsha, a Vêda-versed Brâhmana and priest in Benares, initially refuses alms to Gayaghôsha, then accepts and praises his teaching, enters the monastic order, annihilates Karman through self-control and penance, and reaches the highest perfection.

Brâhmana is an ascetic defined by conduct rather than birth, designation, honor, learning, or outward observance. After entering the order, this person becomes chaste, self-subduing, noninjuring, truthful, and free from taking, sensual desire, greed, property, household ties, and former connections. Living unknown and unattached, the Brâhmana is not defiled by pleasures, attains Nirvâna through chastity, and becomes exempt from all Karman.

The priests claim that Vêda-versed, chaste, sacrificially learned priests should receive food and all they desire. Gayaghôsha teaches that ignorant priests who merely pretend to know sacrifice and hide behind study and penance cannot thereby save themselves or others.
The Vêdas chiefly concern agnihôtra; mere knowledge neither makes a true Brâhmana nor grants liberation, and reliance on sacrifices causes sin.
Sacrifice centers on its purpose; animal binding, the Vêdas, and sacrifices cause sin and cannot save the sinner because Karman is powerful.

is_longs_for a Sramana Righteousness is sought by the Sramana through austerities, study, self-control, proper food, suitable companionship, and seclusion. The dispassionate person who performs all duties removes obstructions to righteousness.

The teaching presents the true sacrifice as spiritual conduct rather than outward ritual. It consists in qualities such as self-control, chastity, knowledge, penance, non-violence, truthfulness, non-possession, and freedom from attachment and Karman.
Correct behaviour causes freedom from all misery; by practising it, many souls have crossed Samsâra.

is_a correct behaviour [consisting of ten parts] The tenfold correct behaviour consists of âvasyikâ, naishêdhikî, âprikkhanâ, pratiprikkhanâ, khandanâ, ikkhâkâra, mithyâkâra, tathâkâra, abhyutthâna, and upasampad.

Monks pay reverence to the Guru at prescribed times, ask what work or study they should undertake, and seek absolution after confessing transgressions. The Guru receives confession and repentance, and obedience and reverence toward the Guru produce discipline, prevent blameable conduct, and support spiritual progress. Service, praise, devotion, and respect toward the Guru lead to commendable results.
Paurushî divides each day and night into four seasonally varying parts, assigning duties including study, meditation, begging-tour, and sleep cessation.
A monk’s day has four Paurushî: study, meditation, begging-tour, then study, alongside inspections, confession, Kâla-pratikramana, and Kâyôtsarga.
A monk divides the night into four Paurushî for study, meditation, sleepless practice, and further study with observances.

Study is undertaken during the first and fourth Paurushî of the day and the first and fourth Paurushî of the night. A monk should study without allowing pains to affect him and should not wake householders.
Meditation is undertaken during the second Paurushî of the day and the second Paurushî of the night. Food may be begged so that a monk can meditate on the Law.

The begging-tour occurs in the third Paurushî of the day. Food and drink may be sought to prevent illness, serve the Guru, follow walking and self-control rules, save life, or meditate on the Law. The monk should contentedly continue his begging-tour whether he receives alms or not.
Twenty-Sixth Lecture directs monks to inspect and clean possessions, almsbowl, lodging, and sanitation place after sunrise, carefully protecting rather than carelessly injuring living beings.

Living Beings are a constituent of the world (Lôka), described by substance, place, time, and development. They comprise six kinds: earth-bodies, water-bodies, fire-bodies, wind-bodies, plants, and animals. Their distinction from Things without life supports a monk’s self-control. Careful inspection matters because building, preparing food and drink, and fire may injure or destroy them. They unfold as beings still in Samsâra, movable or immovable, subtle or gross, with many subdivisions, or as perfected souls (siddhas).
Earth Lives are immovable living beings, subtile or gross and developed or undeveloped, with gross varieties described and lives lasting twenty-two thousand years.
Plants are immovable living beings, subtile or gross and developed or undeveloped; gross developed forms share one body or possess individual bodies lasting ten thousand years.
Kâla-pratikramana is a monk’s prescribed practice, performed after study and in the night’s final quarter, but excluded during almsbowl inspection’s first-quarter period.
Perfected souls are developed into knowledge. Those well versed in sacred lore and possessing much knowledge are worthy to hear the doctrine of salvation.

Faith is a cause of final deliverance, produced by nature, instruction, command, study of the Sûtras, religious exercise, and the Law. Right belief requires acquaintance with truth, devotion to those who know it, and avoidance of schismatical and heretical tenets; it precedes right conduct. Faith may be obstructed or take right, wrong, or mixed forms, while perfected souls, orthodox opinions, and faith in the creed of the Ginas lead toward Bôdhi and escape from the Circle of Births.
Conduct, a cause of final deliverance, destroys all Karman through five forms: avoiding sin, novice initiation, austerity purity, reducing desire, and annihilating sinfulness under Arhat precepts.

annihilates sins [when recited] After reflecting on transgressions, a monk recites the Pratikramana Sûtra and thereby annihilates his sins before reverencing the Guru and performing further Kâyôtsarga.
is_a lecture The Twenty-Seventh Lecture presents Garga’s reflections on bad bullocks and bad pupils. It concludes with Garga leaving the lazy donkeys and practising severe austerities.
is_a lecture section The Bad Bullocks is the title of the lecture. It concerns comparisons between bad bullocks and bad pupils.
Garga, a kind, grave, meditating learned Sthavira and Ganadhara leading a Gana, reflects on flawed things, becomes disheartened by bad pupils, leaves lazy donkeys, and practises severe austerities.

crosses wilderness [when ridden] A car is used to cross a wilderness. When bad bullocks are put before it, they may cause exhaustion, vexation, damage to the goad, the yoke, the pin, or the rope, and may run off.

Bad bullocks tire out a car driver through beating, resist goads, bite or wound their mate, break rope or yoke, make for a young cow, attack furiously, go backward, stand still as if dead, then run off roaring after breaking loose. They are compared with bad pupils yoked to the car of the Law.

Bad pupils lack zeal, prize success, fare, comfort, and anger, and avoid begging or insults. They object, imagine difficulties, oppose superiors, evade errands, and wander as they please. Though instructed, admitted into the order, and nourished, they behave like servants of the king and disperse in all directions.

destroys living beings [beings living in water, corn, or in earth and wood] Food and drink may contain or destroy beings living in water, corn, earth, and wood. A monk should neither cook food and drink nor cause another to cook them.

l: The Road of Penance, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: The Road of Penance, taught by the Ginas, depends on right knowledge, faith, conduct, and austerities; it leads beings to beatitude by teaching monks to stop bad Karman influx and annihilate accumulated Karman.

Right knowledge is a fivefold kind of knowledge, Sruta, Âbhinibôdhika, Avadhi, Manahparyâya, and Kêvala, and one of four causes of final deliverance. It requires right faith and supports virtuous conduct. True knowledge leads toward deliverance as duties remove its obstructions, while Gñânâvaranîya obstructs its forms.
is_a substrate of qualities Substance is the substrate of qualities, while qualities are inherent in one substance. Dharma, Adharma, space, time, matter, and souls are the six kinds of substances.
development is a fivefold description of lifeless things through colour, smell, taste, touch, and figure.
Dharma, a formless thing with divisions and indivisible parts, is co-extensive with world and ever without beginning and end.
Adharma is a formless thing, divided yet indivisible, coextensive with the world and without beginning or end.
Space, a formless thing with divisions and indivisible parts, fills world and Non-world and is ever without beginning and end.
Time is a formless thing existing in the place of time. As a continuous flow it has no beginning or end, but each individual thing has both.

Soul is one of six kinds of substances and exists in infinite number. Its characteristics include knowledge, faith, conduct, austerities, energy, and realisation. Bound by eight kinds of Karman, it turns in the Circle of Births. Through abstentions, discipline, freedom from passions, and the declared mode of life, it becomes free from Âsravas and crosses Samsâra.

The world (Lôka) comprises living beings and nonliving things, with Dharma and Adharma coextensive with it. It contains beings’ places: perfected souls dwell at its top, while subtile earth lives, water lives, and plants occur throughout.
Nine categories trace soul and inanimate things through Karman, merit, demerit, sin and watchfulness, to Karman’s annihilation and final deliverance; belief brings righteousness.
One of the nine truths, annihilation of Karman unfolds through conduct: sages destroy all Karman by control and austerities.
External austerities are practices including fasting and abstinence, one of two austerity kinds; faithfully performing both kinds leads to release.
The Twenty-Ninth Lecture, The Exertion in Righteousness, explains results of seventy-three spiritual practices, virtues, renunciations, disciplines, and stages.

l: The Exertion in Righteousness, Uttaradhyayana Sutra
s: Mahâvîra’s lecture teaches righteous exertion: longing for liberation, disregard of worldly objects, desire of the Law, obedience, and pure meditation, through which exertion destroys Karman and brings perfection, enlightenment, deliverance, and final beatitude.
heard The Exertion in Righteousness [from Mahâvîra] Sudharman reports that he heard this discourse from the venerable Mahâvîra.

Longing for liberation produces an intense desire of the Law and helps the soul abandon wrong belief and destructive passions. Exertion directed toward liberation ultimately leads the soul beyond Samsâra.
Enlightenment follows the destruction of Karman and the attainment of absolute knowledge and faith. The perfected soul obtains enlightenment together with deliverance and final beatitude.

Final deliverance is bliss attained when the soul destroys remaining Karman and rises to the highest Akâsa, accompanying perfection, enlightenment, and final beatitude through true knowledge, avoidance, and destruction.
Eternal beatitude is liberation: destroying Karman and worldly existence, shedding property, egoism, passions, and Âsravas, attaining natural form, absolute knowledge, and misery’s end.
Denizens of hell are beings with five senses, divided among seven named hells, where shortest and longest lifespans increase by hell.
Samvêga is longing for liberation. It produces an intense desire of the Law, helps destroy anger, pride, deceit, and greed, and supports the attainment of right faith and eventual perfection.

are_stopped_by self-denial [as if by closing their doors] Âsravas cease for the soul through abstention from the six specified actions and through possessing the five Samitis and three Guptis, freedom from passions, subduing the senses, vanquishing conceit, and avoiding delusions.

Pure meditation, its third degree relapse-free, requires only the subtlest organ functions and finally stops mind, speech, body, and breathing, annihilating four remaining Karman before the soul rises naturally.
is_a lecture The Thirtieth Lecture explains the Road of Penance and how a monk destroys Karman acquired by love and hatred through austerities.
Bad Karman is stopped by prescribed abstentions and virtues; without its influx, austerities gradually destroy the Karman previously acquired by a monk.
Love and hatred cause Karman, bondage, and misery; arising from attachment or aversion, monks avoid them and austerities destroy them for final deliverance.
Fasting is an external austerity of two kinds: temporary fasting, with six forms, and maranakâla, which ends with death and is classified by bodily motion and permitted relief or departure.

Abstinence is an external austerity of five kinds: substance, place, time, state of mind, and development, involving reduced food, restricted alms collection, specified acceptance, and enumerated particulars.
A monk practises this mode of life for liberation; it benefits the soul and carries many souls across Samsâra.
